metadata.summary: These European practice recommendations address the diagnosis, classification and management of paediatric high-grade gliomas, including diffuse midline, hemispheric and infant-type tumours. They cover imaging and molecular diagnosis, surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and selected investigational approaches for newly diagnosed or progressive disease. The guidance combines available evidence with expert opinion while acknowledging the limited paediatric treatment evidence and differences in resources across European countries.

conditions_covered: Diffuse paediatric-type high-grade glioma, H3-wildtype and IDH-wildtype
target_population: Children and adolescents with paediatric high-grade gliomas
Patients with newly diagnosed or progressive/relapsed disease

toxicities.event: Severe late effects on the developing brain
prevention: Avoid radiotherapy in young children < 2 years with infant-type HGG; it may be considered at relapse in selected cases according to age, prior treatment and molecular subtype.

therapies_index.name: temozolomide (TMZ)
approved_indications: Used with local radiotherapy and as adjuvant treatment for newly diagnosed hemispheric pedHGGs; its use in DMG H3K27-altered lacks consensus.
Should be avoided in pedHGG driven by DNA replication repair deficiency.
therapies_index.administration: During chemoradiation, 75 mg/m2/d continuously from the first through the last radiation fraction. After a treatment break of approximately 4 weeks, adjuvant treatment is given in 28-day cycles: 150 mg/m2/days 1–5 in the 1st cycle, with escalation to 200 mg/m2/days 1–5 from the 2nd cycle if tolerated.
monitoring: Tolerance during the 1st adjuvant cycle determines whether the dose is escalated.

therapies_index.name: lomustine
approved_indications: May be considered as adjuvant therapy for pedHGG driven by DNA replication repair deficiency.
Was combined with TMZ as adjuvant treatment in the ACNS-0423 study.
therapies_index.administration: In ACNS-0423, 90 mg/m2/day on day 1 of each adjuvant cycle, together with TMZ.
monitoring: In ACNS-0423, repeat cycles depended on bone marrow recovery.

therapies_index.name: Stupp regimen
approved_indications: Presented as the preferred chemoradiation and adjuvant chemotherapy approach for diffuse paediatric-type high-grade glioma, H3-wildtype and IDH-wildtype, and diffuse hemispheric glioma H3 G34-mutant, irrespective of MGMT promotor methylation status.
therapies_index.administration: Local radiotherapy with daily continuous TMZ 75 mg/m2/d from the first to the last radiation fraction; after a TMZ break of approximately 4 weeks, adjuvant TMZ for 6–12 cycles. The detailed recommended adjuvant schedule specifies 12 cycles of 28 days: 150 mg/m2/days 1–5 in the 1st cycle, increasing to 200 mg/m2/days 1–5 from the 2nd cycle according to tolerance.
monitoring: Assess tolerance during the 1st TMZ cycle before dose escalation.

therapies_index.name: TMZ-RT
approved_indications: Used for hemispheric pedHGGs; its role in DMG H3K27-altered is disputed.
therapies_index.administration: TMZ is administered concomitantly with radiotherapy; the guideline also describes subsequent adjuvant TMZ.

therapies_index.name: PCV
approved_indications: Studied after radiotherapy and maximal safe surgery in children with HGG in CCG-943 and CCG-945.
therapies_index.administration: Administered after radiotherapy in the cited trials; a drug-by-drug schedule is not specified.

therapies_index.name: 8-in-1
approved_indications: Studied in CCG-945 and reported as treatment for infants with malignant astrocytoma.

therapies_index.name: ICE
approved_indications: Evaluated as neoadjuvant and adjuvant chemotherapy for pedHGGs; brainstem tumours did not benefit in the cited study.
therapies_index.administration: In the cited phase II approach, 4 neoadjuvant courses preceded hyperfractionated RT and 4 adjuvant courses followed it.

therapies_index.name: BBSFOP
approved_indications: One of the recommended chemotherapy regimens for infant-type hemispheric HGG in European countries.
therapies_index.administration: The treatment section describes a 16-month schedule of 7 cycles alternating carboplatin-procarbazine, cisplatin-etoposide and vincristine-cyclophosphamide. An earlier account describes an 18-month schedule.

therapies_index.name: modified-HIT-SKK
approved_indications: One of the recommended chemotherapy regimens for infant-type hemispheric HGG in European countries.
therapies_index.administration: Used without intraventricular methotrexate. The HIT-SKK regimen on which it is based comprises three two-month cycles.

therapies_index.name: HIT-SKK
approved_indications: Described as a strategy to postpone or avoid radiotherapy in young patients with brain tumours; the guideline discusses published outcomes in children with medulloblastoma.
therapies_index.administration: Three two-month cycles including intravenous methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, carboplatin and etoposide. The cited medulloblastoma treatment also included intraventricular methotrexate.

therapies_index.name: UKCCSG/SIOP CNS 9204
approved_indications: Studied as chemotherapy without radiotherapy for infants with non-brainstem HGG.
therapies_index.administration: The trial description lists courses of carboplatin/vincristine, high-dose methotrexate/vincristine, cyclophosphamide monotherapy and cisplatin monotherapy. The later description of the UK version lists cyclophosphamide-vincristine instead of cyclophosphamide monotherapy, states that intraventricular therapy was omitted, and describes chemotherapy every 2 weeks.

therapies_index.name: carboplatin-procarbazine
approved_indications: One of the alternating drug pairs in BBSFOP for infant-type hemispheric HGG.

therapies_index.name: cisplatin-etoposide
approved_indications: One of the alternating drug pairs in BBSFOP for infant-type hemispheric HGG.

therapies_index.name: vincristine-cyclophosphamide
approved_indications: One of the alternating drug pairs in BBSFOP for infant-type hemispheric HGG.

therapies_index.name: carboplatin-vincristine
approved_indications: A course in the UK chemotherapy-only approach for infant HGG.

therapies_index.name: high-dose methotrexate-vincristine
approved_indications: A course in the UK chemotherapy-only approach for infant HGG.

therapies_index.name: cyclophosphamide-vincristine
approved_indications: Listed as a course in the later description of the UK chemotherapy-only approach for infant HGG.

therapies_index.name: cyclophosphamide
approved_indications: A component of chemotherapy regimens discussed for infant HGG.
therapies_index.administration: The initial account of UKCCSG/SIOP CNS 9204 describes a monotherapy course; the later account describes a cyclophosphamide-vincristine course.

therapies_index.name: vincristine
approved_indications: A component of chemotherapy regimens discussed for pedHGG.
therapies_index.administration: Described as weekly during radio-chemotherapy in HIT-GBM-C; other schedules are not specified.

therapies_index.name: carboplatin
approved_indications: A component of chemotherapy regimens discussed for pedHGG, including infant HGG.

therapies_index.name: etoposide
approved_indications: A component of chemotherapy regimens discussed for pedHGG, including infant HGG.

therapies_index.name: ifosfamide
approved_indications: A component of ICE and of the intensive chemotherapy described in HIT-GBM-C.

therapies_index.name: cisplatin
approved_indications: A component of chemotherapy regimens discussed for pedHGG, including infant HGG.
therapies_index.administration: The infant chemotherapy descriptions include a cisplatin monotherapy course.

therapies_index.name: procarbazine
approved_indications: Combined with carboplatin in BBSFOP for infant-type hemispheric HGG.

therapies_index.name: methotrexate
approved_indications: A component of infant brain-tumour chemotherapy regimens described in the guideline.
therapies_index.administration: Described as intravenous in HIT-SKK, as intraventricular in the cited medulloblastoma treatment, and as high-dose methotrexate with vincristine in the UK infant chemotherapy approach. Intraventricular methotrexate is omitted from modified-HIT-SKK for infant-type hemispheric HGG.

therapies_index.name: prednisolone
approved_indications: A component of PCV in the cited childhood HGG trials.

therapies_index.name: bevacizumab
approved_indications: Investigated with TMZ-RT in pedHGG; the Herby trial did not find improved EFS or OS for non-brainstem pedHGG.
Studied alongside re-irradiation in adults, without a survival improvement in the cited report.

therapies_index.name: vorinostat
approved_indications: Investigated during RT in ACNS0822; that experimental arm showed no clear superiority over TMZ/RT.
therapies_index.administration: Given during RT in ACNS0822.

therapies_index.name: valproate
approved_indications: Under investigation with TMZ in HITHGG-2013.

therapies_index.name: valproic acid
approved_indications: Used after maintenance chemotherapy in the cited HIT-GBM-C treatment approach.
therapies_index.administration: Oral, after maintenance chemotherapy in HIT-GBM-C.

therapies_index.name: nivolumab
therapies_index.mechanism: Described as an immune checkpoint inhibitor.
approved_indications: Under investigation with TMZ and radiotherapy in the NIVOGLIO trial for children and adolescents with newly diagnosed HGG.

therapies_index.name: erlotinib
approved_indications: Investigated after biopsy-based biological assessment in BIOMEDE 1.0 for DMG H3K27-altered; no tested agent showed superiority over the others.

therapies_index.name: dasatinib
approved_indications: Investigated after biopsy-based biological assessment in BIOMEDE 1.0 for DMG H3K27-altered; no tested agent showed superiority over the others.

therapies_index.name: everolimus
approved_indications: Investigated in BIOMEDE 1.0 for DMG H3K27-altered and chosen as the standard arm for BIOMEDE 2.0 because it had fewer side effects.

therapies_index.name: ONC201
therapies_index.mechanism: Selective antagonist of dopamine receptor D2/3 (DRD2/3).
approved_indications: Investigational treatment for H3 K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma; after radiotherapy, expanded access may be considered if a clinical trial is not an option. Its preliminary efficacy findings await confirmation.
therapies_index.administration: The expanded-access option described is after radiotherapy; a dose and route are not specified.

therapies_index.name: entrectinib
therapies_index.mechanism: Tyrosine kinase inhibitor described as targeting NTRK, ALK and ROS1.
approved_indications: The guideline states that market authorization limits its use in children to NTRK fusion gene-positive tumours when adequate other treatment options are absent; it states that entrectinib has no market authorization for ALK and ROS1 positive paediatric tumours. Precision medicine is not currently recommended for newly diagnosed infant-type hemispheric HGG.

therapies_index.name: larotrectinib
approved_indications: Under investigation in CONNECT1903 for children with high-grade glioma and NTRK fusion. The guideline states that market authorization limits its use in children to NTRK fusion gene-positive tumours when adequate other treatment options are absent; precision medicine is not currently recommended for newly diagnosed infant-type hemispheric HGG.

therapies_index.name: corticosteroids
approved_indications: Used for symptomatic CNS tumours, including raised ICP, preparation for surgery, symptoms during radiotherapy and long-term palliative symptom control; their use should be restricted.
key_toxicities: Reduced blood–brain barrier permeability and possible impairment of anti-tumour immunity.

therapies_index.name: immune checkpoint inhibition
approved_indications: Described as improving survival at progression in hypermutant gliomas driven by DNA replication repair deficiency; it may be considered upfront for some patients with favourable genomic and immune biomarkers.

therapies_index.name: BRAF/MEK inhibitor
approved_indications: Named as a potential molecularly selected treatment at hemispheric HGG relapse or progression.

therapies_index.name: anti-EGFR therapy
approved_indications: Named as a potential molecularly selected treatment at hemispheric HGG relapse or progression.

therapies_index.name: CDK inhibitor
approved_indications: Named as a potential molecularly selected treatment at hemispheric HGG relapse or progression.

therapies_index.name: maximal safe surgery
approved_indications: The surgical approach for hemispheric pedHGG when resection is possible without lasting, disabling neurological deficits.
key_toxicities: Lasting and disabling neurological deficits are to be avoided.

therapies_index.name: surgical resection
approved_indications: Recommended if feasible at relapse or progression of hemispheric HGG, alongside molecular pathology assessment.

therapies_index.name: biopsy
approved_indications: Recommended when tumour imaging is atypical or when a widespread or inoperable tumour requires histological and molecular verification; may be considered for a radiologically typical pontine DMG outside a trial after discussion with the family.
Often requested by clinical-trial protocols for suspected pontine DMG.
therapies_index.administration: The described approaches include microsurgery, neuroendoscopy, and navigated, stereotactic or robotic needle biopsy.
key_toxicities: A cited meta-analysis of 735 paediatric brainstem tumour biopsies reported permanent morbidity and mortality of 0.6 % each.

therapies_index.name: 5-ALA fluorescence-guided surgery
approved_indications: Described as a technical aid to maximal safe resection.

therapies_index.name: awake surgery
approved_indications: May improve operative safety near eloquent brain regions in selected paediatric cases, although it is difficult to perform in this population.

therapies_index.name: radiotherapy
approved_indications: Used after maximal safe surgery for eligible hemispheric pedHGG and as the principal treatment for DMG H3K27-altered, including palliative treatment of pontine DMG.
Rarely considered for infant-type hemispheric glioma because of severe late effects; it remains an option at relapse in selected cases.
therapies_index.administration: For diffuse paediatric-type HGG in patients ≥ 3 years, local treatment of 54 Gy + /- a boost of 5,4 Gy (1,8 Gy/fraction) to residual disease is proposed. For DMG, the stated standard is 54 Gy in 1,8 Gy by fraction (5 fractions a week). After maximal safe surgery for the specified hemispheric entities, starting within less than 4–6 weeks is recommended.
key_toxicities: Severe late effects in infants and significant adverse effects on the developing brain.

therapies_index.name: Intensity Modulated Radiation Therapy
approved_indications: A simultaneous boost may be proposed to optimize the dose to healthy tissue in the specified diffuse paediatric-type and diffuse hemispheric gliomas.
therapies_index.administration: The proposed simultaneous-boost doses are 54 Gy/1,8 by fraction and 60 Gy/2 Gy by fraction.

therapies_index.name: hypofractionated treatment
approved_indications: An option for pontine DMG to lessen treatment burden, particularly with a Lansky scale of 50–70 and significant neurological symptoms; described as non-inferior to conventional fractionation.
therapies_index.administration: The most-used schedule is 39 Gy in 13 fractions (3 Gy/fraction in 2,5 weeks), without concomitant systemic therapy.

therapies_index.name: hyperfractionated radiotherapy
approved_indications: The guideline states that it has no role in managing diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma; it was used in a cited ICE study of other pedHGGs.
therapies_index.administration: In the cited ICE study, 1.1 Gy twice daily for 30 days.

therapies_index.name: re-irradiation
approved_indications: May palliate symptoms in non-pontine DMG, although evidence and optimal dosing are limited.

For pontine DMG, the guideline describes improved survival and symptoms in more than 2/3 of patients; the best candidates responded to initial treatment and are at least 3 months beyond the first irradiation course.
May be included in multimodal treatment at hemispheric HGG relapse or progression.
therapies_index.administration: For pontine DMG, schedules vary by institution; some data suggest ≥ 20 Gy (1,8–2 Gy/fraction) may be slightly more effective for symptom improvement, while additional benefit from doses up to 36 Gy remains uncertain.

therapies_index.name: CSI
approved_indications: An option for metastatic DMG, including pontine disease, at diagnosis; may also be offered for metastatic relapse after prior radiotherapy.
therapies_index.administration: At metastatic diagnosis, 36 Gy in 20 daily fractions of 1.8 Gy, with an 18 Gy boost in 10 daily fractions to the primary tumour and macroscopic metastases, for a total dose of 54 Gy. At metastatic relapse, 36 Gy in 20 fractions may be offered.

conditions.name: Paediatric high-grade gliomas
conditions.description: A heterogeneous group of invasive gliomas with glial differentiation, classified as CNS WHO grade 3 or 4. Their biology differs substantially from that of adult high-grade gliomas.
conditions.epidemiology: They account for approximately 15 % of central nervous system tumours in children and adolescents. Overall, 5-year survival is less than 20 %.

subtypes.distinguishing_features: Arises in midline structures and includes pontine, thalamic and spinal cord disease.

subtypes.name: Diffuse hemispheric glioma, H3 G34-mutant, CNS WHO grade 4
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A hemispheric entity associated with H3.3 G34R/V.

subtypes.name: Diffuse pediatric-type HGG, H3-wildtype and IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Further molecular subtyping includes pedRTK1, pedRTK2 and MYCN.

subtypes.name: Infant-type hemispheric glioma, H3-wildtype and IDH-wildtype, No CNS WHO grade
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An infant-associated hemispheric entity that can harbour targetable gene fusions.

staging.additional_rules: The document classifies individual molecular entities separately and does not provide an additional staging system.

conditions.name: Diffuse midline glioma H3K27-altered
conditions.description: An infiltrative midline glioma occurring predominantly in the pons, followed by the thalamus and, less often, the spinal cord. Its subgroups share PRC2 inhibition. The disease course associated with H3K27 alteration is uniformly fatal regardless of tumour location.
conditions.epidemiology: The document attributes 10 % of childhood brain tumours and 70 % of childhood HGGs to H3K27-altered DMGs.

subtypes.name: Pontine diffuse midline glioma H3K27-altered (DIPG)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Pontine location; the document describes a distinct imaging-based diagnostic approach.

subtypes.name: H3.3 p.K28M (K27M)-mutant
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Histone H3-mutant subgroup, often associated with PDGFRA and MYC amplifications.

subtypes.name: H3.1 or 3.2 p. K28M (K27M)-mutant
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Histone H3-mutant subgroup, often associated with PDGFRA and MYC amplifications.

subtypes.name: EZHIP overexpression
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A subgroup without an H3 mutation that shows global epigenetic changes consistent with the mutant subgroup.

subtypes.name: EGFR altered
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A subgroup with H3K27me3 loss and frequent EGFR alterations.

special_populations.population: Infants with newly diagnosed high-grade glioma
special_populations.considerations: The guideline uses an age cut-off of 2 years for the infant subgroup, although treatment groups commonly use 3 years. These tumours can differ molecularly from those in older children, and radiotherapy carries a risk of severe late effects on the developing brain. The guideline states that radiation is not recommended in children < 2 years.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Surgery followed by systemic treatment is the usual approach. The recommended chemotherapy options are BBSFOP and modified-HIT-SKK without intraventricular methotrexate; the treating clinician selects a regimen according to institutional circumstances. Molecular analysis should be undertaken if possible to identify ALK, ROS1, NTRK1/2/3 and MET fusions. Targeted treatment is ideally pursued in a clinical trial, but precision medicine approaches are not currently recommended for a new diagnosis of infant-type hemispheric HGG. Radiotherapy is rarely part of initial treatment and may be an option for selected relapses according to age, prior treatment and molecular subtype.

special_populations.population: Patients with germline or somatic DNA replication repair deficiency
special_populations.considerations: This group includes mismatch repair and/or polymerase-proofreading deficiency. Molecular findings may inform consideration of immune checkpoint inhibition.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Focal irradiation is recommended and TMZ should be avoided; lomustine may be considered as adjuvant treatment. decision_rules: Aim for the greatest resection that can be achieved without permanent, disabling neurological injury.

recommended_regimens.name: Maximal safe surgery
recommended_regimens.summary: Resect the hemispheric tumour as extensively as neurological safety permits. Intraoperative MRI, intraoperative ultrasound and 5-ALA fluorescence-guided surgery may help achieve a safe resection; awake surgery may improve safety near eloquent regions in selected children.

recommended_regimens.name: Local radiotherapy
recommended_regimens.summary: For patients aged ≥ 3 years, deliver 54 Gy + /- a boost of 5,4 Gy (1,8 Gy/fraction) to residual disease. With Intensity Modulated Radiation Therapy, a simultaneous boost may instead be proposed at 54 Gy/1,8 by fraction and 60 Gy/2 Gy by fraction. GTV comprises the surgical cavity and postoperative residual disease on T1-contrast, or T2 Flair for a non-enhancing tumour; CTV adds 15 mm within natural anatomical boundaries, potentially reduced to 10 mm for a non-enhancing tumour; PTV adds 2–5 mm according to institutional policy.

recommended_regimens.name: Stupp regimen
recommended_regimens.summary: Give continuous daily temozolomide (TMZ) at 75 mg/m2/d from the first through the last local-radiotherapy fraction. After a TMZ break of approximately 4 weeks, give adjuvant temozolomide at 150 – 200 mg/m2/d: 150 mg/m2/days 1–5 in the 1st cycle, increasing to 200 mg/m2/days 1–5 from the 2nd cycle if the 1st cycle is tolerated. Sixty per cent of Delphi participants supported chemoradiation followed by 6–12 cycles; the specified regimen describes x 12 cycles. ACNS0126 supported its use in newly diagnosed pedHGGs, without establishing a clear efficacy advantage over other chemotherapy agents in subsequent trials.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In ACNS0126, the reported 3-year EFS and OS were 11 ± 7 % and 22 % ± 5 %, respectively.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: TMZ throughout radiotherapy, followed after approximately 4 weeks by 6–12 cycles in the Delphi recommendation; the specified adjuvant schedule is x 12 cycles, with a Cycle length = 28 days.

alternative_regimens.name: TMZ and lomustine
alternative_regimens.summary: Thirty per cent of Delphi participants supported considering lomustine alongside a concomitant and/or adjuvant TMZ backbone. In ACNS-0423, radiotherapy with concurrent TMZ after maximal resection was followed by lomustine 90 mg/m2/day on day 1 and TMZ 160 mg/m2/day on days 1–5, for up to 6 cycles every 6 weeks; cycles resumed every 42 days after bone-marrow recovery. The non-randomized study reported improved outcomes at the cost of greater toxicity, so the proposed MGMT-based rationale remains debated.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An option considered by some Delphi participants for newly diagnosed localised pedHGG; the significance of MGMT expression for predicting response to alkylating agents in pedHGGs is unknown.

document_sections.heading: A B S T R A C T
document_sections.content: Paediatric high-grade gliomas (pedHGGs) are invasive brain tumours comprising approximately 15 % of central nervous system (CNS) tumours in children and adolescents. Their prognosis is generally poor, with 5-year survival rates of less than 20 %. Biological understanding has improved, but effective treatment and outcomes have changed little over the last four decades. Evidence for chemotherapy in children remains weak and is often extrapolated from adults. Developed within the European Standard Clinical Practice (ESCP) Project by the SIOPE HGG Working Group, these recommendations combine available evidence and expert opinion to support healthcare professionals and promote equitable care across European countries with differing resources.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: Paediatric high-grade gliomas (pedHGGs) account for approximately 15 % of CNS tumours in children and adolescents, are highly invasive, and have 5-year survival rates of less than 20 %. Their biology differs significantly from adult disease. The 5th edition of the 2021 WHO CNS tumour classification recognises their heterogeneity. Despite numerous prospective paediatric trials, outcomes have improved little over the past 4 decades. Following surgery and adjuvant radiotherapy, temozolomide-containing regimens have commonly been used as standard treatment and as trial control arms, while clinicians generally seek investigational trial enrolment. Early trials face 4-fold challenges: intertumoural heterogeneity and redundant molecular pathways; absence of actionable alterations in many patients; small populations for individual biological targets; and inadequate drug penetration across the blood–brain barrier. The SIOPE HGG Working Group prepared the guideline for the European Standard Clinical Practice (ESCP) Project. European Reference Networks (ERNs) and European Society for Paediatric Oncology (SIOPE) board members reviewed it before approval for the SIOPE members’ portal. Because access and institutional treatment vary between countries, the guideline combines evidence and expert opinion to assist care and improve equity while accounting for national resources.

document_sections.heading: 2. Classification and previous management approach
document_sections.content: High-grade gliomas (HGGs) are aggressive, glially differentiated tumours defined as CNS WHO grade 3 or 4. Several broad groups occur in children.

document_sections.heading: 2.1. Diffuse midline glioma H3K27-altered
document_sections.content: H3K27-altered diffuse midline gliomas (DMGs) account for 10 % of childhood brain tumours and 70 % of childhood HGGs. They arise in the pons, thalamus or spinal cord. Most have an H3K27 variant and loss of H3K27 trimethylation (H3K27me3), a marker associated with uniformly fatal disease regardless of site. Recognised as a separate entity in WHO 2016, they were subdivided in the 2021 classification. The predominant group carries H3.3 p.K28M (K27M) or H3.1 or 3.2 p. K28M (K27M) mutations, often alongside PDGFRA and MYC amplifications. Smaller groups lack an H3 mutation but show EZHIP overexpression, or have H3K27me3 loss with frequent EGFR alterations. Shared Polycomb Repressor Complex 2 (PRC2) inhibition underlies their grouping in WHO classification 2021. Midline tumours with MYCN amplification (GBM-MYCN) are instead classified within diffuse paediatric-type HGG, H3-wildtype, and IDH-wildtype, subgroup pedHGG MYCN. DMGs were historically managed like hemispheric gliomas. The Children’s Oncology Group (COG) ACNS0126 study found little justification for temozolomide (TMZ) with radiotherapy (RT) in DIPG, now called pontine DMG; its comparison with the earlier CCG-9941 study was not randomised against RT alone, and TMZ-RT was neither inferior nor superior to that study’s intensive pre-RT chemotherapy and hyperfractionation. An analysis of 1130 DIPG patients in the SIOPE and International DIPG registries associated neoadjuvant or adjuvant systemic therapy, mostly TMZ-based, plus RT with longer survival in univariable and multivariable analyses. Wagner et al. retrospectively reported median overall survival (OS) of 11.3 months with chemotherapy after RT versus 9.5 months with RT alone (P = 0.03). Kebudi et al. retrospectively reported significantly higher survival with adjuvant TMZ or other chemotherapy (lomustine, vincristine) than with RT alone; other studies reported findings with intensive neoadjuvant chemotherapy. These non-randomised studies did not define an H3K27-altered DMG subgroup and may be biased. In the randomised Herby trial of non-brainstem midline pedHGG, H3K27M-mutant disease had similarly poor survival (8.0 months OS), without superiority from adding bevacizumab to TMZ-RT. BIOMEDE 1.0, developed in 2014 for H3K27-altered DMG, assigned most patients treatment intended to target a biopsy-identified alteration. Erlotinib, dasatinib and everolimus showed no superiority over one another; respective median OS values were 10.0, 10.5 and 11.9 months. Fewer side effects led to selection of everolimus as the ‘standard arm’ in BIOMEDE 2.0. The SIOPE and International Diffuse Intrinsic Pontine Glioma Registries, established in 2012 and expanded to all DMGs in 2022 and 2019, respectively, collect prospective data and support development of treatment approaches.

document_sections.heading: 2.2. Hemispheric pedHGGs
document_sections.content: Hemispheric pedHGGs comprise 5 % of childhood brain tumours and 30 % of childhood HGGs. Under the 2021 WHO CNS classification they include H3G34R/V diffuse hemispheric glioma, paediatric-type high-grade glioma and infant-type high-grade glioma. The randomised CCG-943 trial, published in 1989, found significantly better outcomes after maximal safe surgery with RT followed by prednisolone/chloroethyl-cyclohexyl nitrosourea [lomustine]/vincristine chemotherapy (PCV) than with RT alone: respective 5-year OS rates were 43 % ( ± 9 %) and 17 % ( ± 7 %). CCG-945 found no significant difference between RT/PCV and eight-drugs-in-1-day (8-in-1), reporting 5-year OS of 36 % ( ± 6 %). Gross total resection (>90 %) was an important survival prognostic factor, and O6-DNA methylguanine-methyltransferase (MGMT) overexpression strongly correlated with worse outcomes in both CCG-945 arms. Central pathology review subsequently found that 30 % of CCG-945 patients had low-grade gliomas misclassified as HGG, producing an adjusted HGG OS rate of 22 % ( ± 3 %); CCG-943 did not undergo equivalent review. An adult glioblastoma trial conducted in 2000–2002 found that TMZ during and after RT significantly prolonged event-free survival (EFS) and OS versus RT alone. MGMT promoter methylation was prognostic, but its ability to predict TMZ benefit has not been prospectively established in children as it has in adults. Paediatric ACNS0126 used TMZ with RT and obtained survival comparable to CCG-945: 3-year EFS of 11 ± 7 % and OS of 22 % ± 5 %. TMZ caused less toxicity than regimens in earlier CCG trials. ACNS-0423 added lomustine to TMZ and reported 3-year EFS of 22 ± 8 % and OS of 28 ± 8 %, with more pronounced findings in patients with MGMT promoter methylation and those without gross total resection, but increased toxicity. In adult MGMT promoter-methylated glioblastoma, CeTeG/NOA-09 found TMZ plus lomustine superior to TMZ alone; its selected population reflected an earlier pilot finding of no observed benefit from adding lomustine in MGMT-unmethylated, MGMT-expressing tumours. The non-randomised phase 2 UKT-03 trial also suggested superiority of lomustine-TMZ plus RT over TMZ chemoradiotherapy in newly diagnosed MGMTp-methylated glioblastoma. In paediatric HIT-HGG-2007, confirmed MGMTp hypermethylation occurred in only 8 out of 183 (4.4 %) patients and moderate methylation in 22 out of 183 (12.0 %); the majority (83.6 %) had unmethylated MGMTp, which did not affect survival with TMZ-RT-based treatment. These findings suggest that MGMTp methylation, unlike in adults, is not associated with survival in children; the cited analysis was submitted but not yet published. ACNS0822 compared vorinostat or bevacizumab during RT with TMZ during RT. Planned as a phase II ‘pick-the-winner’ design preceding phase III, it closed permanently in 2014 during phase II because no arm clearly outperformed TMZ/RT. Adding bevacizumab to TMZ/RT did not improve EFS or OS in the Herby trial of non-brainstem pedHGG, although post-hoc molecular analyses suggested possible benefit in some hypermutated or BRAF-V600E-mutated subgroups. A phase II approach using 4 neoadjuvant courses of ifosfamide, carboplatin, and etoposide (ICE), hyperfractionated RT (1.1 Gy twice daily for 30 days), and 4 adjuvant ICE courses reported low toxicity, 5-year PFS of 56 % and OS of 67 %; brainstem tumours did not benefit. The HIT-GBM-C cooperative study used cisplatin, etoposide, and weekly vincristine during radiochemotherapy, a cycle of cisplatin, etoposide, and ifosfamide in the last RT week, then maintenance chemotherapy and oral valproic acid. Among patients undergoing gross total resection, its 5-year OS was 63 % versus 17 % in a historical control group (P = .003, log-rank test). Absence of molecular data limits interpretation. The ongoing HITHGG-2013 trial compares TMZ plus valproate with historical HIT-HGG-2007 data for TMZ alone. Other investigations include the French phase I/II NIVOGLIO trial of nivolumab with TMZ and RT in newly diagnosed childhood and adolescent HGG.

document_sections.heading: 2.3. Infant-type hemispheric HGG
document_sections.content: Infants with HGG have historically survived longer than older children, including after surgery followed by chemotherapy and, when needed, delayed RT. In CCG-945, infants with malignant astrocytoma given 8-in-1 had 3-year PFS of 36 % and OS of 51 %, substantially better than older children receiving that regimen with RT. Baby POG I, conducted from 1986 to 1996, reported cures using chemotherapy alone for 24 months: two cycles of cyclophosphamide and vincristine alternated with a third cycle of cisplatin and etoposide. Among 18 pedHGG patients, 5-year PFS was 43 % and OS 50 %. The French chemotherapy-only BBSFOP protocol, described here as an 18-month schedule of seven cycles of carboplatin-procarbazine, cisplatin-etoposide and vincristine-cyclophosphamide in children under 5 years, yielded 5-year PFS of 35.3 % and OS of 58.8 %. In UKCCSG/SIOP CNS 9204, infants with non-brainstem HGG received carboplatin/vincristine, high-dose methotrexate/vincristine, cyclophosphamide alone and cisplatin alone; PFS was 13.0 % and OS 30.9 %. Biological differences may contribute substantially to infants’ better outcomes. Many infant tumours, particularly in those under 2 years, differ molecularly from tumours in older children. WHO CNS 2021 recognises ‘Infant-type hemispheric glioma’, and studies identify potentially targetable ALK, ROS1, NTRK1/2/3 and MET fusions.

document_sections.heading: 3. Diagnostic process
document_sections.content: Diagnosis encompasses neuroaxis imaging, selective consideration of CSF analysis and biopsy, and integrated neuropathological and molecular assessment.

document_sections.heading: 3.1. Imaging
document_sections.content: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is central to comprehensive neuroaxis assessment. Baseline imaging and imaging for suspected progression must cover the whole brain and spine. The SIOPE MRI guidelines and the Imaging Working Group’s Standard Clinical Practice Recommendations provide details of essential brain and spine sequences, tumour measurements, postoperative residual-disease definitions and response criteria.

document_sections.heading: 3.2. Role of CSF analysis
document_sections.content: CSF is not routinely collected for pedHGG. Liquid-biopsy applications could make collection relevant in future, but they are not currently standard practice.

document_sections.heading: 3.3. Biopsy in pontine DMGs
document_sections.content: Pontine DMG (pDMG) is conventionally diagnosed from characteristic clinical findings together with MRI appearances. Tissue is not required for diagnosis and management unless age, symptoms, symptom duration or imaging is atypical. Whether to biopsy has long been debated; limited tissue availability has constrained understanding of pDMG biology and may have impeded therapeutic progress. Studies indicate that biopsy is safe when performed by experienced teams. A meta-analysis of 735 paediatric brainstem biopsies reported diagnostic success of 96.1 % and permanent morbidity and mortality rates of 0.6 % each. Navigational robotic technology and other surgical adjuncts can improve precision and safety. BIOMEDE and INFORM required biopsy and obtained adequate material for detailed molecular work with very low adverse-event rates. Emerging trials may increase the value of biopsy for molecular subgrouping, prognosis and eligibility. Most trials now request biopsy for suspected pDMG according to protocol, and the procedure is widely used in neuro-oncology centres without life-threatening complications. Outside trials, biopsy may be considered for a radiologically typical DMG after discussing with the family the potential advantages of histopathological confirmation, possible molecular targeting given emerging subgroup PFS/OS findings, and research uses of remaining tissue. Biopsy is recommended when imaging appearances are atypical.

document_sections.heading: 3.4. Neuropathological diagnosis
document_sections.content: Accurate pedHGG classification and exclusion of histological mimics require immunohistochemistry for cellular lineage and protein surrogates of genetic or epigenetic changes, alongside DNA- and/or RNA-based molecular pathology and methylation-based profiling. Most entities can be defined by specific genetic alterations or characteristic methylation patterns. The diagnostic table relates tumour location, age, IDH and histone 3 status, RTK alterations, mismatch-repair findings and methylome profiles to integrated diagnoses; it includes Diffuse hemispheric glioma, H3 G34-mutant, CNS WHO grade 4; Astrocytoma IDH-mutant CNS WHO grade 3/4; Infant-type hemispheric glioma, H3-wildtype and IDH-wildtype, No CNS WHO grade; Diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-altered, CNS WHO grade 4; and Diffuse pediatric-type HGG, H3-wildtype and IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4. The document also refers to a molecular-characterisation algorithm based on WHO CNS 2021. Differential diagnoses require additional tests: older children and adolescents may have adult-type IDH-mutant astrocytoma, while testing for homozygous CDKN2AB deletions, BRAFV600E and other MAP kinase alterations is recommended when considering pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma. DNA methylation profiling helps confirm diagnosis, subtype H3- and IDH-wildtype HGG, and detect molecular or histological mimics. In infant-type hemispheric glioma and other pedHGG subtypes, suitable RNA- and/or DNA-based testing for ALK, ROS1, MET and NTRK family fusions may identify targeted-therapy candidates. Assessing MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 and PMS2 by molecular methods or immunohistochemistry, or evaluating tumour mutational burden (TMB), may identify patients with germline mismatch-repair deficiency and provide a rationale for immune checkpoint inhibition. The authors recommend MMR-gene IHC when constitutional mismatch repair deficiency syndrome (CMMRD) is clinically suspected, potentially including IDH mutant pedHGG. High-grade IDH-WT diffuse glioma can occur with LiFraumeni syndrome. If molecular testing is insufficient to establish pedHGG type, the designation ‘High-grade gliomas, NOS’ should be used.

document_sections.heading: 4. Treatment
document_sections.content: Management of pedHGG in cancer predisposition syndromes is outside this guideline’s scope. A planned first revision will address it in light of emerging evidence of immunotherapy benefit in these patients.

document_sections.heading: 4.1. Surgery
document_sections.content: Surgery for hemispheric pedHGG aims for the greatest feasible resection without permanent, disabling neurological injury. Adult HGG experience suggests gross total resection improves PFS. Biopsy is recommended to establish histological and molecular diagnoses when tumours are extensive or occupy inoperable eloquent areas such as the pons. Possible approaches include microsurgery, neuroendoscopy and navigated, stereotactic or robotic needle biopsy. Intraoperative MRI, ultrasound and 5-ALA fluorescence guidance can facilitate maximal safe resection. Awake surgery is challenging in children but may improve safety near eloquent regions in selected cases.

document_sections.heading: 4.2. Corticosteroids
document_sections.content: Corticosteroids are commonly given for symptomatic childhood CNS tumours and have recognised uses for increased ICP, surgical preparation, symptom management during RT and long-term palliative relief. Their use should nevertheless be restricted because they reduce blood–brain barrier permeability and may impair antitumour immunity.

document_sections.heading: 4.3. Radiotherapy
document_sections.content: Radiotherapy guidance varies by tumour type and site, including separate approaches to initial irradiation, re-irradiation and metastatic disease.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.1. Diffuse paediatric-type high-grade glioma, H3-wildtype and IDHwildtype and Diffuse hemispheric glioma H3 G34-mutant
document_sections.content: Optimal RT dose and volume have not been evaluated prospectively or retrospectively; earlier recommendations relied on adult experience despite differences in imaging, biology and outcomes. RT is recommended to begin after an interval of less than 4–6 weeks following maximal safe surgery. Multi-institutional studies support proposing local RT for patients ≥ 3 years at 54 Gy + /- a boost of 5,4 Gy (1,8 Gy/fraction) to residual disease. With Intensity Modulated Radiation Therapy, a simultaneous boost may be proposed to spare healthy tissue (54 Gy/1,8 by fraction and 60 Gy/2 Gy by fraction). Gross Total Volume (GTV) comprises the surgical cavity and postoperative residual disease on T1-contrast, or T2 Flair for non-enhancing tumours. Clinical Total Volume (CTV) adds a 15 mm margin constrained by anatomical barriers; the margin may be reduced to 10 mm for non-enhancing tumours. Planning Target Volume (PTV) adds 2–5 mm according to institutional policy. Evidence on re-irradiating non-pontine DMG is sparse; retrospective reports suggest acceptable safety and symptom palliation, but optimal dose, fractionation and volume are unknown. Adult reports found that 35 Gy in 10 fractions with bevacizumab was safe without a survival improvement, and that stereotactic 36 Gy (2 Gy/fraction) produced similar findings. Those reports defined the treatment volume as GTV with a PTV margin.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.2. Diffuse midline glioma H3K27-altered
document_sections.content: Childhood H3K27-altered DMG occurs most often in the pons, next most often in the thalamus, and rarely in the spinal cord. Specific treatment data for non-pontine disease are limited; its current RT recommendations match those for other diffuse paediatric-type high-grade gliomas. In pontine DMG, prompt RT is desirable, but the optimal interval from diagnosis is unknown when a delay is necessary. Starting within 2 weeks does not improve OS. The standard RT dose for all DMG is 54 Gy in 1,8 Gy by fraction (5 fractions a week). For pontine DMG, hypofractionation is proven non-inferior to conventional fractionation. The most-used regimen is 39 Gy in 13 fractions (3 Gy/fraction in 2,5 weeks) without concurrent systemic therapy. It can reduce treatment burden, particularly in children with a Lansky scale of 50–70 and substantial neurological symptoms such as pyramidal tract dysfunction or disequilibrium. Hyperfractionated RT has no role in diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma. GTV encompasses the combined abnormalities on T1-contrast, T2 and Flair. CTV adds 10 mm, bounded by anatomical structures such as the bony calvarium and tentorium; PTV adds a further 2–5 mm according to institutional policy.

document_sections.heading: Re-irradiation of pontine DMG (pDMG)
document_sections.content: Evidence indicates that re-irradiation improves survival and symptoms in more than 2/3 of patients with pDMG. Patients who responded to initial treatment and are at least 3 months beyond their first irradiation course are the best candidates. Dose, volume and fractionation differ among institutions. Some data suggest that ≥ 20 Gy (1,8–2 Gy/fraction) is slightly more effective for symptom improvement; whether doses up to 36 Gy confer further benefit remains uncertain. PTV is usually GTV plus 2–5 mm, with any limited CTV margin left to the radiation oncologist because no consensus exists.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.3. Infant–type hemispheric glioma
document_sections.content: For this guideline, the infant subgroup uses a 2 years cutoff based on neuropathological diagnosis, although treatment age groups usually use 3 years. Management generally consists of surgery and systemic chemotherapy and/or targeted therapy. RT is rarely included because of severe late effects in infants, but may be an option at relapse in selected patients according to age, previous therapy and molecular subtype. No entity-specific RT recommendation is available.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.4. Spinal cord high-grade glioma
document_sections.content: Spinal cord HGG is very rare in children, and H3K27 alterations occur frequently at this site (50–80 %). RT doses are generally lower than for intracranial tumours because of spinal cord tolerance. The stated dose is 45–50.4 Gy (1,8 Gy/fraction), depending on involved cord length and neurological status. Target-volume practice lacks agreement and draws on intracranial HGG experience, with a CTV margin up to 20 mm in the CC direction.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.5. Metastatic DMG
document_sections.content: For any DMG, including pontine disease, metastatic presentation at diagnosis may be treated with CSI of 36 Gy in 20 daily fractions of 1.8 Gy, followed by boosts of 18 Gy in 10 daily fractions to the primary tumour and macroscopic metastases, for a total of 54 Gy. At metastatic relapse after prior RT, CSI of 36 Gy in 20 fractions could be offered. The document reports metastatic relapse in ≥50 % of patients with thalamic lesions.

document_sections.heading: 5. Chemotherapy
document_sections.content: Advances in pedHGG biology have not translated into substantial improvements in treatment or outcomes over the last four decades. Chemotherapy evidence is weak in children and frequently extrapolated from adults. Only a few sufficiently sized randomised trials in newly diagnosed disease have shown benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy. Most children receive it, but no optimal regimen is established. Because evidence does not clearly favour one approach, the SIOPE HGG Working Group surveyed practice in 33 European countries and sought consensus through a Delphi method. Forty-three neuro-oncology experts from 33 countries were invited to participate between December 2021 and March 2022; voting and responses were gathered online.

document_sections.heading: 5.1. Diffuse paediatric-type high-grade glioma, H3-wildtype and IDHwildtype and diffuse hemispheric glioma H3 G34-mutant
document_sections.content: Concurrent daily temozolomide (TMZ) with local RT followed by adjuvant TMZ is widely preferred in European paediatric neuro-oncology. Sixty per cent of Delphi participants supported TMZ chemoradiation, an approximately 4 weeks TMZ break, then 6–12 TMZ cycles regardless of MGMT promotor methylation. Treatment should begin approximately 4 weeks after cranial surgery; trial enrolment after irradiation is an alternative when available. The recommended concurrent schedule gives TMZ 75 mg/m2/d continuously from the first through the last RT fraction. The specified adjuvant schedule gives TMZ 150 – 200 mg/m2/d x 12 cycles: 150 mg/m2/days 1–5 in the 1st cycle, increased to 200 mg/m2/days 1–5 from the 2nd cycle if the 1st cycle is tolerated, with a 28 days cycle length. This ‘Stupp regimen’ derives from an adult newly diagnosed GBM randomised trial showing that adding adjuvant chemotherapy to RT improved median and 2-year survival, with benefit persisting throughout 5 years of follow-up. The single-arm phase II paediatric ACNS0126 study supported the safety and tolerability of concurrent and adjuvant TMZ with RT. Although later comparisons did not establish a clear efficacy advantage over other agents, favourable safety and tolerability supported its continued acceptance. Thirty per cent of Delphi participants favoured TMZ as the hemispheric HGG backbone while considering lomustine, informed by ACNS-0423 survival findings in MGMT-overexpressing tumours relative to ACNS0126. In ACNS-0423, newly diagnosed localised pedHGG was treated after maximal resection with RT and concurrent TMZ, followed by up to 6 cycles of lomustine 90 mg/m2/day on day 1 and TMZ 160 mg/m2/day on days 1–5 every 6 weeks; cycles recurred every 42 days after marrow recovery. The proposed depletion of MGMT by two alkylating agents remains debated because the study was non-randomised, MGMT immunohistochemistry is controversial relative to methylation status, and the predictive importance of MGMT expression for paediatric alkylator response is unknown. For pedHGG driven by germline or somatic DNA replication repair deficiency, including mismatch repair and/or polymerase-proofreading deficiency, focal irradiation is recommended. TMZ should be avoided; lomustine may be considered as adjuvant treatment. Immune checkpoint inhibition is established to improve survival at progression in these hypermutant gliomas and may be considered upfront for some patients with favourable genomic and immune biomarkers.

document_sections.heading: 5.2. Recurrent/progressive hemispheric high-grade glioma, H3-wildtype and IDH-wildtype patients and diffuse hemispheric glioma H3 G34-mutant
document_sections.content: There is no established standard of care for recurrent or progressive hemispheric HGG. All patients should undergo complete restaging and assessment before treatment selection. Evidence supporting particular strategies is limited, predominantly coming from retrospective cohorts with heterogeneous treatments. Following a survey of SIOPE-BTG and GPOH members, the SIOPE HGG Working Group recommends feasible resection at relapse or progression together with molecular pathology to find potential targeted treatments, such as BRAF/MEK inhibitor, anti-EGFR therapy or CDK inhibitor. Patients should enter available clinical trials. Where international cooperative trials are lacking, combining conventional multimodal approaches, including re-irradiation, with molecularly selected targeted treatment is considered reasonable.

document_sections.heading: 5.3. Diffuse midline glioma H3K27-altered
document_sections.content: Evidence does not currently establish a specific chemotherapy strategy for H3K27-altered DMG, making RT the principal treatment. The Delphi process did not reach chemotherapy consensus. Fifty per cent of participants favoured TMZ chemoradiation followed, after an approximately 4 weeks break, by 6–12 TMZ cycles irrespective of MGMT promotor methylation. Their position draws partly on the as-yet-unpublished HIT-HGG-2007 subgroup analysis presented at ISPNO in 2022: non-pontine pedHGG treated with TMZ had a reported 3-month EFS and OS benefit over more intensive cisplatinum-based chemotherapy, with median EFS of 10.7 versus 7.4 months and OS of 19.3 versus 16.2 months, respectively. Other reports also describe TMZ as better tolerated than alternative cytostatic treatment. The other 50 % did not support TMZ for H3K27-altered DMG, noting unpublished results and ongoing subgroup survival analyses; the question remains unresolved. Preliminary evidence suggests activity of ONC201, a selective dopamine receptor D2/3 (DRD2/3) antagonist, in H3 K27M-mutant DMG. Data first presented at ASCO in 2019 reported a 27 % response rate in supratentorial disease, but confirmation is pending. Activity appears more persuasive in adults and non-brainstem DMG; the recruiting BIOMEDE 2.0 trial compares ONC201 with everolimus and subsequently with historical controls. Given the absence of meaningful established treatment and the preliminary efficacy signal, a patient unable to join a trial may qualify for expanded access to ONC201 after RT. Clinicians and patients should recognise that investigational medicines lack established safety and efficacy and carefully weigh potential benefits and risks before pursuing access outside a trial. When biopsy reveals a target, the biological agent should ideally be used in a clinical trial. Otherwise, the clinician may consider individual circumstances and drug risks, inform patients and parents or guardians about experimental status and possible adverse effects, and account for quality of life. Treatment should primarily follow national guidance and be individualised.

document_sections.heading: 5.4. Progressive/relapsed diffuse midline glioma H3K27-altered
document_sections.content: As at initial diagnosis, no chemotherapy standard has been evaluated and agreed for progressive or relapsed H3K27-altered DMG. If biopsy identifies a target for treatment at progression or relapse, the same principles described for newly diagnosed disease apply.

document_sections.heading: 5.4.1. Pontine diffuse midline glioma H3K27-altered (DIPG)
document_sections.content: Numerous systemic chemotherapy studies have failed to demonstrate a significant survival improvement. RT with palliative intent remains the main treatment. A HIT-HGG-2007 subgroup analysis presented at ISPNO in 2022 reported a 2-month EFS benefit with TMZ in pontine pedHGG, with median EFS of 8.2 versus 6.2 months, but no OS benefit: median OS was 11.4 versus 11.3 months. A biopsy-identified targeted biological agent should ideally be administered within a trial. If trial enrolment is impossible, the principles used for other pedHGG apply.

document_sections.heading: 5.5. Progressive/relapsed pontine diffuse midline glioma H3K27-altered
document_sections.content: For a biopsy-identified target considered at progression or relapse, treatment must be regarded as experimental and should ideally take place in a clinical trial. If enrolment is not feasible, the same recommendations described for initial disease apply.

document_sections.heading: 5.6. Infant-type hemispheric HGG
document_sections.content: Chemotherapy without RT is widely preferred for newly diagnosed infant HGG. Seventy-five per cent of Delphi participants agreed that RT should be avoided to prevent substantial harm to the developing brain; RT is not recommended for children < 2 years. Poor outcomes and late effects have reinforced reluctance to irradiate these patients. The two regimens currently recommended in European countries are BBSFOP and modified-HIT-SKK without intraventricular methotrexate. These approaches draw on French BBSFOP, German modified-HIT-SKK and the UK chemotherapy-only UKCCSG/SIOP CNS 9204 strategy. BBSFOP is described here as a 16-month schedule of 7 cycles using carboplatin-procarbazine, cisplatin-etoposide and vincristine-cyclophosphamide. It reported 5-year PFS of 35 % and 5-year OS of 59 %, with median follow-up of 5.2 years and trial inclusion up to 5 years of age. Its combination of drugs with acceptable infant and young-child toxicity aimed to sustain relatively mild chemotherapy and postpone or avoid RT. HIT-SKK seeks to delay or avoid RT through three two-month cycles containing intravenous methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, carboplatin and etoposide. Published outcomes concern medulloblastoma in children under 4 years; treatment combined with intraventricular methotrexate in young medulloblastoma patients was feasible and well tolerated. Infant-type hemispheric HGG is frequently treated with modified HIT-SKK without intraventricular methotrexate. The UK regimen omitted intraventricular therapy and used carboplatin-vincristine, high-dose methotrexate-vincristine, cyclophosphamide-vincristine and cisplatin alone. It reported 5-year PFS of 18.1 % and 5-year OS of 34.7 % in patients under 3 years. Alternating drugs with different cytotoxic mechanisms, including myelosuppressive and relatively non-myelosuppressive courses, was intended to limit early resistance and permit chemotherapy every 2 weeks. Because European trials included different ages, which affect survival, and preceded molecular classification, clinicians should choose among regimens according to institutional circumstances. Molecular groups of infant HGG have distinct survival. Where possible, tumours should be analysed for ALK, ROS1, NTRK1/2/3 and MET fusions to identify potential trial-based targeted treatment. Entrectinib targets NTRK, ALK and ROS1; encouraging STARTRK-1 findings prompted the paediatric phase 1/2 STARTRK-NG study. Findings in 16 non-infant paediatric patients with primary CNS tumours (median age > 5 years) were promising. The recruiting CONNECT1903 pilot is assessing larotrectinib safety and efficacy in NTRK-fusion HGG. Infant gliomas are mostly single-driver tumours and therefore may suit targeted treatment, but preliminary findings await confirmation. Market authorisation for entrectinib and larotrectinib limits their use in children with NTRK fusion gene-positive tumours to situations without adequate alternative options, whereas infant HGG has such alternatives. Entrectinib also lacks market authorisation for paediatric ALK- or ROS1-positive tumours. Precision-medicine approaches are therefore not currently recommended for newly diagnosed infant-type hemispheric HGG.

document_sections.heading: 6. Conclusion
document_sections.content: Evidence supporting treatment recommendations for childhood pedHGG is limited. Ongoing prospective research addresses an unmet neuro-oncology need. Adapting adult recommendations to children is difficult and can unintentionally result in inappropriate care. Further studies should investigate the biology and treatment of this rare disease group.
